impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the six-year statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for claims against the government in the Court of Federal Claims is subject to American Pipe tolling based on a prior class action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that 28 U.S.C. § 2501 is not subject to American Pipe tolling, recognizing that a portion of its earlier decision in Bright v. United States has been implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's decision in California Public Employees' Retirement System v. ANZ Securities, Inc. This means pendency of a class action does not toll the limitations period for individual Tucker Act claims against the federal government.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides certainty for the government (and by extension government contractors and regulated entities) that stale claims will not be revived through American Pipe tolling, limiting the window of financial exposure for government-related claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Businesses and individuals with claims against the federal government cannot rely on the filing of a class action to toll the § 2501 statute of limitations, requiring them to independently file timely claims or risk permanent forfeiture.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 for method-of-treatment claims requires the specification to enable the full breadth of the claimed genus of antibodies, or whether enablement of representative species suffices.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding broad method-of-treatment claims reciting 'anti-CGRP antagonist antibody' for treating headache. Judge Dyk's dissent argued the panel's holding creates confusion about enablement standards for method claims and will sustain overly broad claims that undermine medical innovation, contrary to Supreme Court precedent in Amgen.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical and biotech patent holders benefit from a more permissive enablement standard for method-of-treatment claims, potentially allowing broader claim scope and stronger patent protection for antibody-based therapies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitor pharmaceutical and biotech companies face broader blocking patents on method-of-treatment claims, potentially increasing litigation risk and limiting freedom to operate with different antibodies targeting the same biological pathway.

impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB's Penumbra framework—which dispenses with the written description analysis required by Dynamic Drinkware for determining a reference patent's prior art date under AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(d)(2)—is correct.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness determination and remanded, addressing the critical issue of when a reference patent may claim a provisional application's filing date as its prior art date under the AIA. The court examined the Board's Penumbra rule, which allowed a reference to receive an earlier priority date based on less rigorous requirements than the written description standard applied under pre-AIA law in Dynamic Drinkware.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from a potentially more rigorous standard for establishing prior art dates of reference patents, making it harder for IPR petitioners to use provisionally-filed references as prior art against patents with intervening filing dates.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on inter partes review to challenge competitor patents may face difficulty establishing prior art status of references whose provisional applications do not fully support the relied-upon disclosures, increasing the cost and uncertainty of patent challenges.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether copyright infringement damages against the government must be assessed by deferring to the terms of an existing license agreement, and what constitutes a proper hypothetical negotiation and 'book of wisdom' analysis for government copyright infringement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the trial court's use of a hypothetical negotiation framework rather than deferring to the existing license agreement to assess copyright damages, but vacated the damages award because the trial court adopted a legally impermissible view of the 'book of wisdom' doctrine and assessed non-compensatory damages against the government. The case involved the government's unauthorized copying of TETRA® software beyond its license terms.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and copyright holders dealing with government agencies benefit from confirmation that damages are not capped by the terms of the original license when the government exceeds its license scope; the hypothetical negotiation framework may yield higher damages.
impacts.negativeImplications: The ruling introduces constraints on damages methodology: courts cannot use the 'book of wisdom' to award non-compensatory damages, which may limit recovery in some government copyright infringement cases and creates uncertainty about proper damages calculations.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive patent license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' sufficient to allow the licensee to sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether the agreement terminated when the licensee shifted its business to enforcement activities.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that the license agreement between Texas A&M and TexasLDPC conveyed all substantial rights in the asserted patents, entitling TexasLDPC to sue without joining A&M. The court also held that TexasLDPC had not ceased business operations merely by shifting to patent enforcement, so the agreement had not automatically terminated.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent licensing entities and exclusive licensees gain clarity that an exclusive license conveying substantial rights—including the right to enforce and sublicense—can constitute a virtual assignment, allowing suit without joining the patent owner. This facilitates patent monetization structures.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose the ability to challenge standing based on non-joinder of the patent owner when the exclusive license conveys all substantial rights; companies may also find it harder to argue that a licensing entity's shift to enforcement constitutes cessation of business triggering license termination.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and what standards apply to damages evidence in patent infringement cases involving standard-essential technology.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the eligibility determination for certain asserted patent claims while affirming eligibility for others, drawing distinctions between claims directed to abstract mathematical optimization and claims tied to specific technical implementations. The court also affirmed the jury's infringement and damages findings, upholding admission of damages expert testimony in a case involving communication standards technology used in televisions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies holding patents on improvements to communication standards gain clarity on when such claims survive § 101 challenges, particularly when tied to specific technical implementations rather than abstract mathematical concepts. The damages ruling supports robust expert testimony on patent value.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies implementing communication standards face continued patent infringement exposure, and the split eligibility ruling creates uncertainty about the line between patent-eligible technical improvements and abstract mathematical optimizations in standards-related patents.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Egyptian Goddess framework for design patent infringement improperly focuses on differences between designs rather than overall similarity, and whether functionality determinations in design patent claim construction present jury questions.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing in a design patent infringement case, with a significant dissent from Chief Judge Moore arguing that the Egyptian Goddess framework has been misapplied to improperly resolve infringement at summary judgment by focusing on design differences. The concurrence defended the current framework as consistent with Supreme Court and circuit precedent.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of design patent infringement benefit from the continued ability to obtain summary judgment of non-infringement when designs are sufficiently distinct, providing an efficient mechanism to resolve design patent disputes without trial.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent holders face a framework that critics argue over-emphasizes differences between designs at the summary judgment stage, potentially making it harder to enforce design patents and reducing their commercial value as IP assets.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has appellate jurisdiction over a contract dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent settlement agreement phrase 'survives the EPR,' or whether the dispute is a state law contract matter belonging in the regional circuit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute about whether T-Mobile owed a contingent payment under a patent settlement agreement, because the core question was contract interpretation under Texas law rather than a substantial patent law question. The case was transferred to the Fifth Circuit.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies negotiating patent settlement agreements gain clarity that disputes over contractual payment obligations will be resolved in regional circuits applying state contract law, which may provide more predictable outcomes and familiar procedural frameworks.
impacts.negativeImplications: Parties who draft patent settlement agreements with payment terms contingent on PTO proceedings face jurisdictional uncertainty; such disputes may end up in regional circuits less familiar with patent reexamination procedures, potentially affecting contract interpretation.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court properly awarded attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 and sanctioned plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927 after dismissing a patent infringement complaint with prejudice and denying leave to amend as futile.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal of a patent infringement suit, the denial of leave to amend, and the award of attorney fees and sanctions against plaintiff's counsel. The court found the case was exceptional under § 285 and that counsel's conduct warranted sanctions, reinforcing that pursuing frivolous patent infringement claims—particularly after the plaintiff implicitly agreed not to amend—can result in significant fee-shifting and personal sanctions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the court's willingness to award fees and impose sanctions in cases involving meritless patent infringement claims, deterring strike suits and reducing the cost burden of frivolous patent litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent plaintiffs and their counsel face heightened risk of fee-shifting and personal sanctions when bringing infringement claims that are dismissed as futile, particularly where related patents have been rejected on eligibility grounds or the plaintiff's litigation conduct is questionable.

impacts.caseName: Archroma U.S., Inc. v. Department of Commerce
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulatory 15-day filing deadline for domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in antidumping duty sunset reviews conflicts with the governing statute, 19 U.S.C. § 1675(c).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade and upheld Commerce's 15-day regulatory deadline for domestic interested parties to indicate participation in sunset reviews of antidumping duty orders. The court found the statute silent on the deadline and the regulation a permissible exercise of agency authority, reversing the Trade Court's invalidation of the regulation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic manufacturers and producers benefit from a structured timeline for sunset reviews, as the upheld 15-day deadline ensures prompt initiation of reviews that could maintain protective antidumping duties against foreign competitors.
impacts.negativeImplications: Importers and foreign exporters face a procedural framework that facilitates continuation of antidumping duties, as domestic parties have a clear and upheld regulatory pathway to participate in sunset reviews that may maintain trade-restrictive orders.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims reciting a 'communications apparatus for transmitting electric or electromagnetic signals over air' with a coupler matching impedance to air are invalid for lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), even though the district court had found them indefinite.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's indefiniteness ruling but affirmed the final judgment of invalidity on alternative enablement grounds. The court held that while the claims were sufficiently definite, they were not enabled because the specification did not teach a person of ordinary skill how to practice the full scope of the claimed invention, which encompassed scientifically impossible embodiments.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies defending against broad patent claims can raise enablement as an alternative invalidity defense even when indefiniteness arguments fail, providing additional avenues to invalidate overly broad patents that claim scientifically impossible subject matter.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders with broadly drafted claims face the risk that courts will invalidate their patents on enablement grounds even after surviving indefiniteness challenges, highlighting the importance of ensuring specification support matches claim breadth.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court must provide sufficient detail in denying a motion for sanctions under Rule 11 and attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 to permit meaningful appellate review, particularly where related patent claims were rejected under § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's denial of sanctions and attorney fees, holding that the court's order provided insufficient detail for meaningful appellate review. The case involved a patent infringement suit brought after the PTO had rejected related application claims under § 101 following Alice, and after a related patent had been invalidated by another court on the same ground.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers gain stronger footing to seek fee-shifting in cases where plaintiffs pursue infringement claims despite clear § 101 invalidity signals from the PTO and related litigation, as courts must provide reasoned explanations for denying such motions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent plaintiffs and their counsel face increased scrutiny and potential fee liability when bringing suits on patents whose related applications were rejected under § 101, with courts now required to articulate detailed reasoning when denying fee petitions.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may dismiss a patent infringement case on § 101 patent eligibility grounds after already concluding that venue is improper and dismissing on that basis.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dual dismissal—for both improper venue under 28 U.S.C. § 1400(b) and patent ineligibility under § 101—holding that a court may properly reach the merits of patent eligibility even after determining venue is improper. The '979 patent related to e-commerce methods using a 'bridge computer' for facilitating transactions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the ability to obtain merits-based dismissals (including § 101 ineligibility) even when venue is also improper, potentially preventing re-filing in a proper venue and providing broader issue-preclusion protection.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face the risk that a single court can simultaneously dismiss for venue and reach the merits to invalidate claims, foreclosing the opportunity to re-file in a proper venue with the patent intact.

impacts.caseName: KG Dongbu Steel Co., Ltd. v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Court of International Trade erred in sustaining Commerce's determination, made under protest after remand, that certain debt-to-equity conversions conferred no countervailable benefit under 19 U.S.C. § 1677(5).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed and reinstated Commerce's original determinations that debt-to-equity conversions by a Korean steel company constituted countervailable subsidies. The court rejected the trial court's repeated remands that had forced Commerce to change its determination, holding that Commerce's original equityworthiness analysis was proper.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic steel manufacturers and other industries benefit from the reinstatement of Commerce's original subsidy findings, which support the imposition of countervailing duties that protect against unfairly subsidized foreign competition.
impacts.negativeImplications: Foreign manufacturers and importers face restored countervailing duties based on Commerce's original subsidy determinations, increasing the cost of imported goods and reducing their competitive advantage in the U.S. market.
